old: This word for a mechanical worker was invented for a 1920s stage play, not borrowed from everyday speech.
Its Czech root means forced labor or drudgery, coined by the writer Karel Čapek.
That root is related to an old Slavic word for slave — English has no native relatives for it at all, making this one of the few everyday words borrowed wholesale from Czech.
clues: This name for a kind of machine was coined by Czech writer Karel Čapek for a 1920 stage play, from a Slavic word for forced labor or drudgery.
A programmable machine that carries out tasks on its own, such as welding cars or vacuuming floors. Unlike an android, it needn't look human at all.
R2-D2 and WALL-E are beloved movie examples, and a person who works mechanically, without feeling, is sometimes called one too.
